bib.title: RLAIF vs. RLHF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, Vienna, Austria. PMLR 235, 2024

question: Can an off-the-shelf LLM replace human annotators as the preference source for RL alignment with comparable policy quality?
hypothesis: LLM-generated preference labels are a viable substitute for human labels; higher AI labeler alignment should lead to better RLAIF policies.
contributions: RLAIF achieves comparable performance to RLHF on summarization, helpful dialogue and harmless dialogue.
RLAIF improves over an SFT policy when the labeler is the same size as the policy or the exact same checkpoint.
d-RLAIF derives reward directly from an off-the-shelf LLM during RL and matches or outperforms canonical RLAIF.
Study of techniques to maximize alignment of AI preferences to human preferences.

method.summary: AI preference labels come from PaLM 2 prompts (log-prob softmax over '1' vs '2', averaged over both candidate orders). A reward model on PaLM 2 XS is trained on soft labels and a REINFORCE-with-baseline policy is trained, compared with the same pipeline on human labels. d-RLAIF skips the RM and uses a 1-10 LLM score as reward.
method.task: preference-based RL alignment (summarization, helpful and harmless dialogue)

datasets.name: Reddit TL;DR (filtered)
datasets.split: train rollout prompts, test for human eval

datasets.name: OpenAI human preferences (TL;DR)
datasets.split: AI labeling on 15% downsample of train, high-confidence only (confidence 1,2,8,9), 3-4k examples

datasets.name: Anthropic helpful-base and harmless-base
datasets.split: test split into 2/3 validation and 1/3 test; AI labeling on 10% downsample of train (3-4k)

models.name: PaLM 2 XS (SFT)
models.init_from: summarization: fine-tuned on Reddit TL;DR; other tasks: instruction-tuned PaLM 2 XS

other.params_note: parameter count not given in the paper

other.default: PaLM 2 L; XS for same-size RLAIF and d-RLAIF

models.name: Reward models (human and AI feedback)
models.init_from: summarization: AI RM from SFT model, human RM from PaLM 2 XS; dialogue: both from instruction-tuned PaLM 2 XS

training.objective: RM: cross-entropy on softmax of RM scores with soft AI labels (Bradley-Terry style loss for human labels); policy: REINFORCE with value baseline, KL penalty to SFT, objective (1-beta)r - beta*KL
training.batch_size: SFT 128; RM 128 summarization and 32 other tasks; RL 128
training.epochs: SFT 1 epoch; RM 2-3 epochs until plateau; RL 8 epochs
training.seq_len: SFT max input 1024 and output 128 tokens; RM 1152 tokens

other.checkpoint_selection: 4 high-reward candidate checkpoints, judged by an off-the-shelf LLM win rate vs SFT plus manual inspection of a dozen examples
other.post_processing: trailing symbols removed from summaries (App H)

inference.decoding: CoT rationale for labeling: greedy, T=0.0, max 512 decoding tokens
inference.temperature: 0.0 for labeling CoT; 0.3-1.0 for self-consistency; 0.9 for RL policy sampling
inference.samples: two inferences per pair (candidate order swapped) averaged; self-consistency 4 or 16 samples (2 or 32 inferences)
inference.prompting: Preamble (Base or Detailed), optional few-shot exemplars, sample, ending; optional two-step CoT

parameters.d_rlaif_score: s(y|x)=sum_i i*P(i|y,x) over tokens 1-10, normalized to [-1,1]
parameters.best_prompts: summarization Detailed + CoT 0-shot; helpfulness Base + CoT 0-shot; harmlessness Base 2-shot

metrics.name: AI labeler alignment
metrics.definition: fraction of examples where argmax of soft AI preference equals the human preference

metrics.name: Win rate
metrics.definition: percentage of instances where humans prefer policy A over B; rankings without ties

metrics.name: Harmless rate
metrics.definition: percentage of responses rated harmless independently by humans

metrics.name: RM pairwise accuracy
metrics.definition: RM scores preferred candidate higher on a holdout set of human preferences

eval.protocol: Human raters (~2k rating instances, ~6k context-response pairs, 3 raters each, ~18k tuples; Kendall W 0.6-0.7); significance via binomial test, paired and two-sample t-tests; single run per condition, seeds not stated.

availability.weights: PaLM 2 available through Vertex AI but exact reproducibility not guaranteed
availability.data: public datasets: Reddit TL;DR, OpenAI preferences, Anthropic hh-rlhf

prompts.text: You are an expert summary rater. Given a piece of text and two of its possible summaries, output 1 or 2 to indicate which summary is better.

You are an expert summary rater. Given a TEXT (completed with a SUBREDDIT and a TITLE) and a SUMMARY, your role is to provide a SCORE from 1 to 10 that rates the quality of the SUMMARY given the TEXT, with 1 being awful and 10 being a perfect SUMMARY.
First, discuss the helpfulness and honesty of each response. Then, explain which one is better overall and why. Finally, select which response is the most helpful and honest. Rationale:
Consider the coherence, accuracy, coverage, and overall quality of each summary and explain which one is better. Rationale:

evidence.quote: We use the Adafactor optimizer with a learning rate of 10−5.

results.claim: RLAIF is preferred over SFT on summarization (71%) and RLHF is preferred over SFT (73%); difference not significant.
results.setup: Summarization, Reddit TL;DR test split. Human evaluation, test splits, SFT/RL policies from PaLM 2 XS, AI labels from PaLM 2 L (best prompt per task), canonical RLAIF (RM + REINFORCE)
results.quote: RLAIF and RLHF are preferred by human evaluators over the baseline SFT policy 71% and 73% of the time for summarization6 and 63% and 64% for helpful dialogue generation, respectively.

results.claim: RLAIF vs SFT 63% and RLHF vs SFT 64% on helpful dialogue; head-to-head RLAIF vs RLHF 52% (not significantly different from 50%).
results.setup: Helpful dialogue (Anthropic helpful-base test). Human evaluation, test splits, SFT/RL policies from PaLM 2 XS, AI labels from PaLM 2 L (best prompt per task), canonical RLAIF (RM + REINFORCE)
results.table: Table 1, row RLAIF vs RLHF, column Helpful dialogue (52%); rows RLAIF vs SFT 63%, RLHF vs SFT 64%

results.claim: RLAIF vs RLHF head-to-head on summarization is 50%.
results.setup: Summarization; Human evaluation, test splits, SFT/RL policies from PaLM 2 XS, AI labels from PaLM 2 L (best prompt per task), canonical RLAIF (RM + REINFORCE)
results.table: Table 1, row RLAIF vs RLHF, column Summarization

results.claim: On harmless dialogue RLAIF scores a higher harmless rate than RLHF and SFT, statistically significant by two-sided paired t-tests.
results.unit: harmless rate (RLAIF vs RLHF vs SFT)
results.setup: Harmless dialogue (Anthropic harmless-base test); humans rate each response harmless/harmful independently; AI labels from PaLM 2 L with Base 2-shot prompt.
results.quote: For harmless dialogue generation, RLAIF achieves a harmless rate of 88%, outperforming both RLHF and SFT, which score 76% and 64%, respectively7.

results.claim: After post-hoc length control, summarization win rates drop (RLAIF vs SFT 59%, RLHF vs SFT 61%) but RL policies still beat SFT by similar margin. Policies were longer than SFT (164, 161, 132 chars).
results.setup: Summarization; logistic regression on length ratio, predicted at ratio 1.0; method conceded to be imperfect.
results.quote: our length-adjusted win rates for RLAIF and RLHF vs. SFT are 59% and 61%, respectively (see Table 8).

results.claim: Length-controlled harmless rate: RLAIF 91%, RLHF 78%, SFT 64%.
results.setup: Harmless dialogue, SFT average length as reference.
results.table: Table 10, rows SFT/RLHF/RLAIF, column Length corrected

results.claim: Same-size RLAIF (PaLM 2 XS labeler, XS policy) is preferred over SFT 68% of the time vs 71% for PaLM 2 L labeler; difference not significant (two-sample t-test p=0.07).
results.setup: Summarization only. The XS labeler is instruction-tuned XS while the policy is XS fine-tuned on TL;DR, so the authors say it is not strict self-improvement.
results.quote: Same-size RLAIF still improves greatly over the SFT baseline, with human annotators preferring same-size RLAIF 68% of the time over SFT (see Table 1).

results.claim: d-RLAIF beats SFT 74% on summarization and 66% on helpful dialogue; the helpfulness case uses the same checkpoint as labeler and initial policy (strict self-improvement).
results.setup: Summarization and helpfulness; d-RLAIF labeler is instruction-tuned PaLM 2 XS, scoring 1-10 directly during RL.
results.quote: For helpful dialogue generation, we find that d-RLAIF achieves a a win rate of 66% over the SFT baseline.

results.claim: d-RLAIF is preferred over same-size RLAIF head-to-head 60% (significantly different from 50% by binomial test) on summarization; same-size RLAIF vs SFT is 68% against d-RLAIF 74%.
results.setup: Summarization, PaLM 2 XS labeler in both arms; differ only in reward function (direct score vs distilled RM).
results.table: Table 1, row d-RLAIF vs Same-size RLAIF, column Summarization

results.claim: Length-controlled d-RLAIF vs same-size RLAIF falls to 56%; d-RLAIF vs SFT 65%, same-size RLAIF vs SFT 59%.
results.setup: Summarization
results.table: Table 11, rows d-RLAIF vs Same-size RLAIF, column Length corrected

results.claim: AI labeler alignment rises with labeler size on summarization: PaLM 2 L 78.0%, S 73.8%, XS 62.7%.
results.setup: Summarization, Detailed + CoT 0-shot prompt (best prompt), 3-4k downsampled filtered preference examples; alignment vs human preferences.
results.table: Table 3, rows PaLM 2 L / S / XS, column AI Labeler Alignment

results.claim: Position bias grows as labeler shrinks: % same position preferred after swapping is 18% (L), 21% (S), 56% (XS).
results.setup: Summarization, Detailed + CoT 0-shot.

results.claim: Best prompts beat Base 0-shot by +1.9%, +1.3%, +1.7% alignment for summarization, helpfulness, harmlessness.
results.setup: PaLM 2 L labeler; Table 2 prompt variants.
results.quote: The best prompts outperform the base prompts (“Base 0-shot”) by +1.9%, +1.3%, and +1.7% for summarization, helpfulness, and harmlessness, respectively.

results.claim: Summarization alignment is 78.0% for Detailed + CoT 0-shot vs 76.1% for Base 0-shot.
results.setup: Summarization, PaLM 2 L.
results.table: Table 2, rows Detailed + CoT 0-shot and Base 0-shot, column Summary

results.claim: CoT helps summarization consistently but for helpfulness/harmlessness only with Base preamble; in-context exemplars lower alignment for summarization and helpfulness (Detailed 8-shot summarization 69.8%) and help only harmlessness (Base 0-shot 69.4% to Base 2-shot 72.1%).
results.setup: PaLM 2 L, Table 2.
results.note: Authors verified with 10 random 1-shot exemplar trials on summarization: max alignment 76.1%, below Base 0-shot.
results.table: Table 2, row Detailed 8-shot, column Summary (69.8%); row Base 2-shot, column Harm. (72.1%)

results.claim: Self-consistency (16 sampled CoT rationales, preference distributions averaged) lowers alignment, 72.8% at T=1.0 vs 78.0% with greedy single sample.
results.setup: Summarization, Detailed + CoT 0-shot, top-K sampling K=40; 4 vs 16 samples differ by up to 0.4%.
results.note: Text says 'see Figure 14' but the data are in Table 14.
results.table: Table 14, rows 1 sample T=0.0 and 16 samples T=1.0, column AI Labeler Alignment

results.claim: LLM labeler agreement of 78% compares with human inter-annotator agreement of 73-77% on the OpenAI summarization preference data.
results.setup: Summarization; human figure is from Stiennon et al. (2020), not measured here.
results.quote: Stiennon et al. (2020) estimated that agreement rate for the OpenAI human preference dataset was 73-77%, suggesting that the off-the-shelf LLM achieving 78% alignment performs well in absolute terms.

results.claim: Policy trained on Detailed CoT 0-shot labels (78.0% alignment) is preferred 59% over policy trained on Base 0-shot labels (76.1%); only two policies compared.
results.setup: Summarization, RLAIF; authors say rigorous experimentation is required.
results.quote: human evaluators prefer summaries from “Detailed CoT 0-shot” 59% of the time over “Base 0-shot”17.

results.claim: Reward models trained on human feedback are more accurate than those trained on AI feedback on held-out human preferences, yet RLAIF matches or beats RLHF.
results.unit: % pairwise accuracy (human RM vs AI RM)
results.setup: Pairwise accuracy on human holdout.
results.note: RMs trained on Base 0-shot vs Detailed CoT 0-shot labels score 77.9% vs 74.2%, the inverse order of RL outcome; RM accuracy may not reflect RL usefulness.
results.table: Table 5, rows Summarization 79.3% vs 74.2%, Helpful 76.0% vs 67.8%, Harmless 72.1% vs 69.7%

results.claim: Combining human and AI feedback (RLHF + RLAIF) did not improve over RLHF alone: 71% vs 74% win rate over SFT, not significant.
results.setup: Summarization; RM trained on human labels plus PaLM 2 L AI labels.
results.quote: RLHF + RLAIF and RLHF achieve win rates of 71% and 74% over SFT, respectively.

results.claim: AI preference labeling is estimated over 10x cheaper than human labeling: $0.06 vs $0.67 per example.
results.setup: Summarization labeling with GPT-4 list prices (not PaLM 2) vs Google Cloud human annotation prices at time of writing; excludes annotator training and setup costs.
results.note: Per-example cost $0.06 AI vs $0.67 human (304 words * $0.11/50 words).
results.quote: We estimate AI preference labeling to be over 10x less costly than human preference labeling following the calculations below.

results.claim: Human evaluators prefer RLAIF and RLHF over human reference summaries 79% and 80% of the time.
results.setup: Reddit TL;DR.
results.quote: RLAIF and RLHF are also preferred over the human reference summaries in Reddit TL;DR 79% and 80% of the time, respectively.

results.claim: Qualitative: RLHF summaries sometimes hallucinate where RLAIF does not; RLAIF summaries sometimes less fluent. A 70-example blind ranking showed no significant difference.
results.setup: Summarization, small-scale human inspection.
results.quote: We conducted a small-scale evaluation on 70 examples, where human annotators were asked to blindly rank RLHF and RLAIF summaries in terms of accuracy, coverage, and coherence.

limits: PaLM 2 only, policies all PaLM 2 XS; parameter counts and compute not reported; no seeds or variance across runs.
Human win rates are sensitive to length; post-hoc length correction is conceded to be imperfect (App J).
End-to-end sensitivity to labeler alignment compares only two policies; authors say rigorous experimentation is required.
Qualitative differences (RLHF hallucination, RLAIF fluency) not shown significant at scale.
Combining human and AI feedback showed no gain in the one setup tried.
Same-size RLAIF is not strict self-improvement; strict case is d-RLAIF on helpfulness only.
Cost estimate uses GPT-4 and Google Cloud list prices, not PaLM 2 cost.
Impact statement: AI labels may transfer biases; human experts should be gold standard in high-stakes domains such as medicine, law, employment.
SHP dataset gave no meaningful improvement over SFT for either RLHF or RLAIF after length correction (App J mention), so results are not universal.
RL uses REINFORCE rather than PPO; results may differ with other RL algorithms.
